newsitem.title: USA: Chrysler to spend $400 mln to move operations.
newsitem.headline: Chrysler to spend $400 mln to move operations.

text.p: The United Auto Workers tentative pact with Chrysler Corp mirrors terms of the Ford Motor Co agreement, but also commits Chrysler to spend $400 million to relocate its Jeep and Truck engineering group.

The move, which will occur in 1999, will add 550 existing salaried Chrysler workers to the UAW's membership rolls at the company. The union represents about 60,000 hourly and 6,000 salaried workers at the automaker.
Details of the agreement were provided to reporters on Thursday at a meeting of the UAW-Chrysler National Council, which is expected to approve the tentative deal.

The Jeep and Truck engineering unit, now located on Plymouth Road in Detroit, will be relocated to a new facility to be built at the Chrysler Technology Center in Auburn Hills, Mich. The unit is the former engineering center for American Motors Corp, which Chrysler bought in 1987.
Economic terms of the contract, as expected, provide job security guarantees and economic gains of more than $13,900 for hourly UAW members at Chrysler.
For hourly workers, Chrysler agreed to make lump sump payments of $2,000 in the first year, followed by three percent base wage gains in the second and third years.

UAW salaried workers at Chrysler will receive gains of up to $15,400 under the tentative pact. That includes a lump sum payment of $2,000 in the first year, salary increases of three to four percent in the second year, and a three percent increase in the third year.
Chrysler has about 6,000 salaried workers represented by the UAW, the most of any of the U.S. Big Three automakers.

Like Ford, Chrysler agreed to keep 95 percent of its UAW workforce during the three-year deal. It also received the same permission from the union to temporarily shrink its workforce more than that in the event of a severe economic downturn.

Also similar to Ford, the agreement allows Chrysler to eliminate some jobs as new technology and processes make plants "We've never argued against technology, all the way back to the Walter Reuther days," said UAW Vice President Jack Laskowski, referring to the long-time UAW leader.
"We firmly believe that technology, in a way, creates jobs," Laskowski told reporters before briefing plant level leaders on the pact.
The agreement also gives Chrysler some flexibility to adjust its work force within certain plant groups located in a given geographic area.
